title: Forming Questions
summary: Ask yes/no and information questions naturally with intonation, word order, and question tags.

sections.heading: Yes/no questions
sections.body: In Brazilian Portuguese, yes/no questions usually keep the same word order as statements. In speech, intonation does the work; in writing, use a question mark at the end.

sections.heading: Questions with question words
sections.body: Question words normally come at the beginning, but everyday speech can also place them at the end for clarification or surprise.

examples.note: common in speech, often asking for clarification

sections.heading: Short answers and tags
sections.body: Portuguese often answers with the verb or a short phrase. Tags like **né?**, **certo?**, and **tá?** check agreement, but they are informal.

examples.en: Do you like coffee? I do.
Is he coming today? Yes, he is.

keyPoints: Yes/no questions usually keep statement word order.
Intonation signals questions in speech; punctuation signals them in writing.
Question words can appear at the beginning or, informally, at the end.
Short answers often repeat the verb instead of using sim alone.

commonMistakes.note: Portuguese does not use do/does for questions.
Subject before verb is the normal Brazilian pattern.
Né? is the natural informal tag.
